changes.before: With no user argument, what happens?
changes.after: Command-line arguments give a program text when it starts. Check how many arrived before reading one.

before: In the hosted main form, argc gives the argument count and argv points to strings. argv[argc] is a null pointer, not another argument string. This program requires exactly one user argument. Launch ./app C for the worked output topic=C; this gives argc == 2.

Read argv[1] only after checking the count. Shell quoting decides which text reaches the program as one argument; C itself receives the resulting strings. Numeric options still need explicit parsing and validation, as in the earlier strtol lesson.
Expected output or behavior: topic=C. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Pass a quoted two-word topic and distinguish one string argument from two. You may trace it without a C compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A command-line argument is text given when starting a program. argc counts the supplied argument strings. In a normal launch, argv[0] holds the program name and argv[1] is the first user argument. argv[argc] is a null pointer marking the end.
This program requires argc to be 2: the program entry and one topic. It checks that before reading argv[1]. Numbers received this way are still text and need parsing before arithmetic.
Run `./app C` on Linux or macOS, or `.\app.exe C` in Windows PowerShell. The topic argument is C, so the program prints topic=C.
With no topic, the count check prints usage: app TOPIC and returns failure. Shell quoting can keep a topic containing spaces together as one argument; the program receives the resulting strings.
